mainEntity.name: How much does a Mercedes E Class 270 CDI engine replacement cost in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: Supply-only rebuilt OM612 or OM647 engines range from £1,900 to £3,200 depending on engine code and condition. With specialist fitting, budget £2,300-£4,000 total. OM612.961 (E 270 CDI, 170 hp, 1999-2002): rebuilt £1,900-£2,800. OM647.961 (E 270 CDI, 177 hp, 2002-2005): rebuilt £2,000-£3,200. OM648.961 (E 300 CDI, 204 hp, 2002-2006): rebuilt £2,200-£3,500. Labour adds £400-£800 depending on specialist location.

mainEntity.name: What are the signs of 'Black Death' injector failure in an E Class 270 / 300 CDI?

acceptedAnswer.text: Visible black, crusty carbon deposits around the injector bases under the engine cover - along with a diesel smell in the cabin or engine bay. Hard, tar-like carbon buildup around one or more injectors is the classic sign. May be accompanied by a chuffing sound from the leaking injector seal. If ignored, injectors can seize in the head, requiring specialist extraction. Early replacement of seals (£350-£550 at a specialist) prevents costly head damage.

mainEntity.name: Is it worth replacing the engine on an older E Class 270 CDI or 300 CDI?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if the car is otherwise sound. The OM648 straight-six in particular is highly regarded for its durability and smoothness, making preservation worthwhile. A quality rebuilt OM647 or OM648 costs £2,000-£3,500 supply only. W211 examples with good service history still command £2,500-£6,000 used. A replacement engine with warranty costs less than financing a newer car. Specialist fitting adds £400-£800, not dealer rates of £1,500+.

mainEntity.name: What is the most reliable engine in the E Class 270 / 300 CDI range?

acceptedAnswer.text: The OM648 3.2-litre straight-six is widely regarded as one of the most durable diesel engines Mercedes ever built. OM648 features a cast iron block and DOHC valvetrain. Power output of 204 hp and 500 Nm torque. Known for exceptional smoothness and longevity. Replaced by the OM642 V6 in 2006, which introduced oil cooler seal issues.

mainEntity.name: What causes injector failure in the OM647 and OM648 engines?

acceptedAnswer.text: Injector seals degrade over time, allowing combustion gases to leak past. The Common Rail fuel system operates at very high pressure, requiring careful maintenance. Copper sealing washers fail, causing 'Black Death' carbon buildup. Injector offset values require correct programming. Using low-quality diesel fuel accelerates injector wear. Injector replacement should be done with new seals and hold-down bolts.

mainEntity.name: How long does a Mercedes E Class 300 CDI engine last?

acceptedAnswer.text: With proper maintenance and 8,000-10,000 mile oil changes, OM648 engines regularly reach 300,000-400,000 miles. Many examples exceed 500,000 km in taxi and fleet use. OM648 straight-six bottom end is near-indestructible. Injector seal replacement at 80k-150k miles is the key maintenance item. Regular oil changes are critical for turbocharger longevity. The OM648 is considered one of Mercedes' most durable engines ever produced.

historyTimeline.h2: Mercedes Benz E Class 270 CDI / 300 CDI - Engine History & Specs at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: The E 270 CDI and E 300 CDI badges represented Mercedes-Benz's five-cylinder and six-cylinder diesel offerings across the W210 and W211 E-Class generations. The E 270 CDI used the OM612 and OM647 2.7-litre inline-five turbodiesels, while the E 300 CDI utilised the OM648 3.2-litre straight-six - the last of the legendary inline-six diesels before the V6 OM642 era.

milestones.description: **1999** - W210 E 270 CDI launched with OM612.961 2.7-litre five-cylinder turbodiesel, 125 kW (170 hp)
**1999-2002** - OM612.961 fitted to W210 E 270 CDI saloon and estate
**2002** - W211 E 270 CDI launched with updated OM647.961 engine, 130 kW (177 hp)
**2002-2005** - OM647 DE 27 LA fitted to W211 E 270 CDI (130 kW / 177 hp)
**2002** - W211 E 300 CDI launched with OM648.961 3.2-litre straight-six diesel, 150 kW (204 hp)
**2002-2006** - OM648 fitted to E 300 CDI and E 320 CDI models
**2005** - OM648 production ends; replaced by OM642 V6 diesel
**2009** - W211 production ends; W212 generation introduced

commonProblems.h2: Mercedes E Class 270 CDI / 300 CDI Engine Problems - Repair Cost vs Replacement
commonProblems.h3: The OM612, OM647, and OM648 engines that power the E Class 270 CDI and 300 CDI are among the most robust diesel engines Mercedes ever produced - properly maintained examples regularly exceed 300,000 miles. However, injector seal failure ("Black Death") dominates replacement enquiries across all three engine families. Every rebuilt engine supplied through EnginesMarket includes upgraded components designed to address the original failure point, plus a minimum 12-month unlimited mileage warranty. Below, we break down what these failures cost to fix and when replacement is the smarter option.

problems.h4: "Black Death" Injector Seal Failure - Why E Class 270 / 300 CDI Diesel Engines Suffer Prematurely
problems.affectedModels: Mercedes E Class 270 CDI / 300 CDI (OM612, OM647, OM648, 1999-2006)
problems.rootCause: The copper injector sealing washer degrades over time, allowing combustion gases to escape past the injector. This creates hard carbon deposits - the characteristic "Black Death" - that can weld injectors into the cylinder head. Injector seals cost as little as £1 each, but labour and specialist tools make the repair significantly more expensive.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Removal of injectors, cleaning of injector bores, new copper seals and stretch bolts
repairOptions.longevity: 60,000-80,000 miles; effective if caught before carbon buildup becomes severe

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Stuck injector removal (may require specialist extraction tools), thread repair, new seals and injectors if damaged
repairOptions.longevity: 100,000+ miles; necessary when injectors are seized in the head

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Supply & fit of rebuilt OM612/OM647/OM648 with new injectors, seals and upgraded components
repairOptions.longevity: When injector damage has compromised the cylinder head or engine has suffered consequential damage

problems.vehicleValueCheck: A typical W210 E Class 270 CDI is worth £1,500-£4,000 depending on condition and mileage; a W211 example typically commands £2,500-£6,000【INDUSTRY ESTIMATE】. If the vehicle is worth under £3,000, a used engine or minor injector seal repair is usually the pragmatic choice. For W211 cars worth £4,000+, a rebuilt engine with warranty can be justified if the rest of the car is sound.
problems.recommendation: Injector seal replacement is almost always the right first step if caught early - the £350-£550 specialist cost is far less than the £2,000+ bill for a seized injector removal and head repair. If "Black Death" has been ignored and the injectors are seized, weigh the cost of head repair against a rebuilt engine. On a W211 E 300 CDI with good bodywork and transmission, a rebuilt engine often makes more sense than a costly extraction job. The OM648 is a particularly desirable engine - its straight-six smoothness and durability make it worth preserving.
problems.cta: -> Compare rebuilt OM612 / OM647 / OM648 Mercedes E Class 270 / 300 CDI engine prices

problems.h4: Turbocharger & Glow Plug Issues - The OM647 and OM648 Secondary Weaknesses
problems.affectedModels: Mercedes E Class 270 CDI / 300 CDI (OM647, OM648, 2002-2006)
problems.rootCause: The variable geometry turbocharger (VNT) can suffer from sticking vanes due to carbon buildup from soot. Glow plugs can fail, causing cold-start difficulties and increased emissions. The Common Rail fuel system requires high-pressure maintenance.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Turbocharger strip, clean, and rebuild or replacement
repairOptions.longevity: 100,000+ miles; when VNT vanes are sticking

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Supply & fit of rebuilt engine with new turbo and ancillaries
repairOptions.longevity: When turbo failure has caused engine damage

problems.vehicleValueCheck: (Same as above - W210 £1,500-£4,000; W211 £2,500-£6,000). On cars worth over £4,000, addressing turbo and glow plug issues promptly prevents more serious damage.
problems.recommendation: Glow plug replacement is a straightforward job at a specialist. Turbocharger issues should be diagnosed early - sticking vanes can be cleaned, but if ignored, turbo failure can send debris into the engine. If caught early, the £500-£900 specialist turbo repair is excellent value.
